activity: how social, economic and environmental systems influence one another
knowledge_domain: how social, economic and environmental systems influence one another
fact: China's campaign to kill sparrows, launched in 1958, removed a predator of crop-eating insects, and locust swarms that followed contributed to the Great Chinese Famine.
story:
The seminar room smelled of wet coats and radiator dust, and the projector showed a photo of the Fulton Street community garden with its pea rows chewed down to stubs. Maika sat with her notebook open to a page she had filled at two in the morning, because last week the garden committee, which included Tyrell's mother, had voted to tear out the hedges and put up netting to keep every bird out of the beds. The vote had passed by one. She had until Saturday to change their minds, and Mr. Clarke had offered her the last fifteen minutes of his Thursday seminar to make her case, on the condition that she treat it as a real argument, not a plea.

She stood up too fast and her chair scraped. "The hedges are where the wrens nest," she said. "The wrens eat the insects that eat the peas. If we clear the birds out, we clear out the ones working for us." Steve, who had argued for the netting since April, put his hand up before she finished.

"You don't know that," he said. "Maybe the insects come anyway. Maybe the wrens eat seeds too. We lost forty percent of the pea crop." He had numbers; she had structure. She could feel the difference between those two things, and how the room leaned toward numbers.

"I did know something," she said, and turned to the whiteboard, because this was the part she had practiced. She had found it in the library's ecology section on Tuesday, chasing a footnote about pest outbreaks, and she had read the page three times with a pencil in her hand. "In 1958, China launched a campaign to kill sparrows. Everyone thought the sparrows were stealing grain. They killed them off, millions of them, and it turned out the sparrows had been eating crop-eating insects. With the sparrows gone, locust swarms followed, and those swarms contributed to the Great Chinese Famine." She wrote the year on the board and set the marker down. "They solved the problem they could see and emancipated the one they couldn't."

Mr. Clarke, who had promised to say nothing, kept the promise, though she saw him straighten slightly at the last sentence. Tyrell leaned forward with his elbows on the table. His mother had cast the deciding vote, and until this moment he had defended it on the grounds that a garden feeding eleven families couldn't afford poetry. "So what do you want," he said slowly, "netting on some beds and open hedges near them?"

"Beds with netting for the seedlings," Maika said. "Hedges left standing, and open rows after the plants are established. The birds become deterrence against the insects, not an enemy we pay to exclude." She heard herself say deterrence and hoped it sounded like a plan rather than a vocabulary word.

Steve was quiet for a long moment, and the room waited, and the rain ticked against the window. Maika thought of her grandmother's allotment back when Maika was nine, the summer before the family sold the house. Her grandmother had walked the rows every evening with a torch and a jar, picking caterpillars off the kale by hand, and when Maika asked why she didn't just spray, her grandmother had said, "The birds come if I leave the edges wild, and they do this for free." Maika had forgotten that for three years, until Tuesday, reading about locusts in a library that smelled nothing like kale. She had put the book flat on the table and sat very still, because the footnote and the memory were the same fact wearing different clothes.

"Fine," Steve said finally. "I'll withdraw the motion for total netting if you put it in writing that the open rows are your responsibility. If the insects take them, that's on you." It was a hard offer and a fair one. She said yes before she could weigh it properly, and only afterward felt the weight settle, the possibility that she was wrong, that the local birds and local insects might not behave like China's had, that a system could be real in one place and not another. She did not say any of that aloud. She wrote it in her notebook instead, under the heading Uncertainties, because she wanted it on record somewhere.

On Saturday the committee met in the garden itself, standing in the drizzle between the chewed pea rows and the hedge full of unseen nests. Tyrell's mother read the revised motion aloud, looked at the hedge for a while, and raised her hand to vote. The wrens, indifferent to procedure, went on working the branches behind her, and one dropped to the fence post near Steve's elbow, carrying something small and green in its beak.

activity: to direct a one-act play by blocking the actors' movements and running rehearsals
knowledge_domain: to direct a one-act play by blocking the actors' movements and running rehearsals
fact: Countering is when one actor shifts position to balance the stage after another actor crosses, keeping both visible to the audience.
story:
The auditorium they'd been assigned for round two had emptied by noon, when the debaters scattered to the cafeteria and the library to sharpen their cases, and Jayden had chosen to spend the break the way he'd spent every break for two weeks: staging his one-act in the corners other people forgot. Alanna and Chiara had agreed to run lines with him before their own rounds, which meant he had forty minutes and two actresses who would only tolerate so much.

"Again from the crossing," he said, and dropped into the third row of seats, the audience's-eye view Mr. Bondarenko had told him to occupy rather than directing from the stage. "Chiara, when you go to the table, don't wait for me. Just move."

Chiara crossed toward the table on the line about her father's letters, exactly as scripted, and Alanna turned to follow her with her whole body, angling downstage, and Jayden watched the moment happen: Chiara passed in front, Alanna shifted a half-step to her left, and the two of them settled into a balance that kept both faces open to him. He hadn't asked for that. He'd been fighting this problem for days.

"Hold it," he said. "Right there. Alanna, what did you just do?"

"I got out of the way so she wouldn't block me." She shrugged, script curled in one hand. "You keep telling us we disappear."

"Say that again. The word. You countered."

"Fine, I countered. Can we move on? I'm supposed to be negating agricultural subsidies in ninety minutes."

Jayden got out his phone and typed it before the sentence could desiccate in his memory, the way his directing notes always did, drying out into fragments that meant nothing by Thursday. Countering, he wrote, one actor shifts position to balance the stage after another actor crosses, keeping both visible to the audience. He read it back and felt the small, private satisfaction of a name arriving for something he'd only seen as fog.

He thought about the fall, then, because the fall was the reason any of this was happening. He'd been the one who wanted to act, the one Mr. Bondarenko had cast as Juror Eight, and he'd been intransigent about his line readings right up until the night he realized the other six people on stage were arranging themselves around him like furniture around a stubborn piano. He'd quit the cast and asked to direct instead, and he still wasn't sure whether that had been maturity or retreat. His father said quitting was quitting. His mother said knowing your weight in a room was a kind of talent. Neither had watched him rehearse.

"Okay," he said, standing. "Chiara, you cross on the letters line. Alanna, you counter, downstage left, so we hold both of you. Then we flip it. Alanna crosses, Chiara counters. Same shape, different sides."

They ran it. It worked, or nearly: Chiara's counter came a beat late and left her half-hidden behind Alanna's shoulder for two full lines, and Jayden called it out from the seats without softening it, because he'd decided that his job was not to be liked. "You're gone," he said. "I can see Alanna's earring and none of you. Watch her feet, not her face."

"I was watching her face because that's what acting is," Chiara said, but she ran it again, and this time the shift came on the breath before the line, and the stage balanced itself so cleanly that Jayden forgot to write it down. He just sat there in the empty auditorium, in the dust and the smell of the debate tournament drifting in from the hallway, someone's extemporaneous speech about the debt ceiling being delivered with great certainty two doors down, and he understood something he couldn't yet say in a note. The movement wasn't decoration on top of the acting. The movement was an argument the two bodies were making about who mattered in the scene, and if the argument was wrong, the best line reading in the world collapsed into bathos, the letters about her dead father landing like a grocery list.

At least he thought that was it. He was seventeen and had directed nothing that an audience had paid to sit through, and it was possible that Mr. Bondarenko would hear his theory and point out some tradition of blocking that said the opposite. He was willing to find that out. That, he suspected, was the difference between him now and him in the fall: the willingness.

"Time," Alanna called, gathering her file of evidence cards. "Subsidies await."

"Thank you," Jayden said. "Both of you. Genuinely."

"Thank me by not putting me behind a plant in the actual show," Chiara said, shouldering her bag, and then she was gone through the double doors, and Alanna was gone, and the auditorium was his.

He sat back down in the third row, opened his notebook, and drew the stage as a rectangle. He drew Chiara's cross as an arrow. He drew Alanna's counter as a second arrow, curving to meet it, and looked at the two lines for a long moment before writing underneath, in handwriting he hoped he'd still be able to read by Thursday: this is the shape. Then he stood, walked down to the stage, and moved the table two feet upstage right.

activity: to give honest feedback to a teammate in a way that is specific and kind
knowledge_domain: to give honest feedback to a teammate in a way that is specific and kind
fact: Researcher Amy Edmondson described 'psychological safety' in 1999 as a team's shared belief that it is safe to take interpersonal risks, such as admitting a mistake.
story:
Nicholas set the table wrong again, forks on the left when his mother wanted them on the right, and he didn't notice until she reached across him to swap two of them without comment. He was thinking about Hunter, who had spent three evenings building the code for their robotics project and had, somewhere in those evenings, made an error so obvious that Nicholas had spotted it in ninety seconds. Nobody else on the team had said a word. Not Gregory, who had definitely seen it. Not the ninth-grader who barely spoke anyway. At Tuesday's meeting they had all nodded along while Hunter explained his logic, and the whole room had performed confidence in something none of them believed, and Nicholas had said "looks good" with the rest of them. He kept turning that over, the way you press a bruise.

At dinner his father asked how the robot was coming, and Nicholas said the code had a problem, then stopped. His sister was telling some story about her own friends, something about a girl who had lied about a party, and nobody had called her on it either. His mother said people avoid things like that, it was human nature, and Nicholas heard himself say, half to his own plate, that it was more specific than that. "There's this researcher," he said. "Amy Edmondson. In 1999 she called it psychological safety. A team's shared belief that it's safe to take interpersonal risks, like admitting a mistake." His father looked up, interested. "So when it's missing," Nicholas went on, "nobody admits anything. Nobody on my team would say they saw the error, because they were afraid of looking foolish. Including me. I said looks good." That last part came out of him before he had decided to release it, and the table went quiet in the particular way that meant everyone was choosing what to do with it.

"And now you have to unsay it," his mother said.

He pushed the potatoes around his plate. He had been telling himself all week that he was the honest one on the team, the one who said what he thought, but the evidence was equivocal, to put it mildly. One instance of telling the truth about a broken projector did not outweigh an evening of pretending. He wondered whether a person could be honest in general and dishonest in the moment, or whether the moment was the only place honesty actually lived. His sister said, maybe unhelpfully, that Hunter's feelings would be hurt either way, so he might as well pick the version where the robot worked. His father said, also unhelpfully, that in his office people critiqued each other constantly and it was like a knife fight. Nobody was giving him what he wanted, which was a formula.

What he wanted, he realized on the walk to Hunter's house the next afternoon, was to say the true thing without paying for it. He wanted to be the teammate who speaks up and also the friend who never makes anyone wince. Hunter opened the door holding a screwdriver, delighted to see him, delighted in a way that made Nicholas's rehearsed sentences dissolve. They sat on the garage floor with the robot between them, and Hunter talked through the code with real pride, pointing at his while loop, his variable names, all of it, and Nicholas watched him and thought: he built this. Three evenings. There was nothing to subjugate here, no ego to put down; the mistake was sitting inside the work like a stone in a shoe, and Hunter had walked miles on it without feeling it.

"Hunter," Nicholas said. "The motor logic is good. The way you handle the sensor input, that's cleaner than what I would have written." That part was true and he said it first on purpose, not as a cushion but because it was where his attention had actually gone. "But the loop resets the counter every pass, so the distance calculation starts from zero each time. That's why it drifts left." He made himself point at the exact line. "It's two lines to fix. I checked."

Hunter looked at the screen for a long moment. Nicholas braced for the wince, the coldness, the thing he had been afraid of naming because naming it would make him the kind of person who feared his friend's face. Instead Hunter said, quietly, "Nobody told me that on Tuesday."

"I know. I said looks good." Nicholas kept his voice level. "I saw it before the meeting and I didn't say anything because I didn't want to be the guy who dumps on your work after you stayed up with it. That was wrong of me. Gregory saw it too, I think."

Hunter turned back to the code, scrolling, and Nicholas could not read his shoulders. Maybe this was the start of it, the safety Edmondson had written about, or maybe it was just one moment and the team would go quiet again the second stakes rose. He didn't know yet. He watched Hunter's hand move to the keyboard, delete the counter reset, and type two careful lines. "Run it," Hunter said, and pushed the robot toward the open garage door.

activity: taking a first driving lesson
knowledge_domain: taking a first driving lesson
fact: A blind spot is an area around a car the driver cannot see from the seat, even with mirrors, which is why drivers turn their heads to check before changing lanes.
story:
The parking lot of Bianchi's Driving Academy smelled like burnt coffee and old vinyl, and Jayden sat in the driver's seat with his hands at ten and two, exactly the way the pamphlet had shown. Behind him, in the second row of the training car, Rowen and Kason were arguing about whether the written test was harder than the road test, which was easy for them to argue about since they had both passed the written one on Tuesday. Jayden had passed it too, third try, though he hadn't told them that part.

"Okay," said Mr. Bianchi, settling into the passenger seat and setting his clipboard on his knee. "Parking lot first, then we'll take her out on Milberry Road. Mirror check before anything."

Jayden adjusted the rearview mirror, then the left one, then the right. He had read the manual cover to cover twice, which was more than he could say for either of his friends, and he had done it at the kitchen table late at night while his mother slept, because if she had seen him studying it she would have asked questions he did not want to answer. He put the car in drive and eased out of the space without stalling, which felt like a small victory, and Kason gave a low whistle from the back.

"Smoooooth," Kason said, and Rowen laughed.

Milberry Road was two lanes each way, and at four in the afternoon it moved in slow, turbid pulses, everything gray and brake-lit and closer together than Jayden had expected from the diagrams in the manual. He kept his eyes forward and his speed at the limit and told himself the road was just a bigger parking lot. Mr. Bianchi said nothing, which Jayden chose to read as approval, though he couldn't be sure. A car's silence, he was learning, could mean several things.

"Next light, we'll get in the left lane," Mr. Bianchi said. "There's a turn at the far side of the plaza."

Jayden nodded. He signaled early, the way the manual said, and checked the left mirror. The lane beside him looked empty. His father would have said he was overthinking it, that a mirror was a mirror and you looked at it and that was that, and Jayden had spent a lot of his life half-believing that kind of certainty, the way you half-believe a coin someone else has already flipped. He began to turn the wheel.

"Head check," Mr. Bianchi said, quietly, not alarmed.

Jayden turned his head and there was a sedan, gray and patient, sitting beside him in a spot the mirror had never shown, close enough that he could see the driver's knuckles on the wheel. He straightened the car back into his lane and the sedan slid past and merged ahead of them as if nothing had happened, and Jayden's heart was going like a fist on a door.

"Blind spot," Rowen said from the back, and Jayden was grateful to him for saying it, because he couldn't have.

"I saw," Jayden said. His voice came out steadier than he'd earned. "The mirror doesn't cover it. You have to actually look."

"Exactly," Mr. Bianchi said, and made a small note on the clipboard, and that was all the ceremony the moment got.

They made the turn at the plaza, looped through a quiet residential street, and came back out on Milberry, and the second time Jayden changed lanes he turned his head first, deliberately, before the signal even, and the lane was empty and he moved into it clean. It was the first thing in the lesson that felt like his. The mirrors had lied to him, or rather they had told only part of the truth, and the fix was simple and awkward: you had to stop trusting the machine for one second and look with your own head, which felt reckless and was the opposite.

Kason's phone buzzed in the back and he read it and went quiet in a way that wasn't like him. "Hey," he said after a moment. "Was your brother's car gray? There's one just like it back there."

Jayden watched the road. He had not told Rowen or Kason why he'd waited a year past his birthday to start lessons, why he'd needed three tries at the written test when every question had seemed to include the word collision, why his mother slept so early these days. He had figured the want itself was enough of a reason to be here, and that the rest could stay where he'd put it. But Kason was looking at him in the mirror, at the sliver of him the mirror did show, waiting.

"Yeah," Jayden said. "It was." He checked the rearview, signaled, and turned his head to look.

activity: moving to a new town and leaving old friends behind
knowledge_domain: moving to a new town and leaving old friends behind
fact: The 1967 Holmes and Rahe stress scale lists a change in residence as a stressful life event worth 20 points, the same as a change in schools.
story:
Sierra had told everyone, including herself, that the party was a formality. Two hours in the backyard of Zaynab's house, paper lanterns sagging in the humidity, a playlist Malak had made titled Songs Sierra Pretends Not to Love, and then done. She was not sad. She had said so eleven times since Tuesday, and she was keeping count, which she chose not to examine.

"You're doing the thing," Zaynab said, handing her a cup of punch that tasted like every party they'd ever been to. "The hostess thing. You're refilling bowls nobody needs refilled."

"That's called being helpful." Sierra took the cup anyway. "Somebody has to make sure the chips migrate to the far table."

Malak appeared from behind the folding table with his phone out. "Okay, so I fell down a rabbit hole last night, and it's weirdly relevant. There's this thing, the Holmes and Rahe stress scale, from 1967. Psychiatrists made a list of stressful life events and gave them point values. Changing residences is on it. Twenty points."

"Twenty out of what?"

"Out of a hundred, for like a total stress load, whatever. But here's the kicker. A change in schools is also on the list. Also twenty points. Exactly the same." He turned the screen toward her as if it were evidence in a trial only she was on trial for. "Moving house and changing schools are tied. Same weight."

"Great," Sierra said. "I'm doing both. So I'm forty points of tired, that's all it is. It's practically medical." She laughed, and Zaynab did not, and the laugh atrophied somewhere in her throat, folding in on itself before it finished.

Ms. Li, who lived next door and had come over with a plate of almond cookies and no intention of leaving early, was stacking cups by the fence. "You should keep that list," she said mildly, to no one in particular, and went back to stacking. Sierra watched her for a second, then turned back to her friends before the silence could mean anything.

Zaynab pulled her toward the far corner of the yard, past the wilting balloons, and said, in a voice pitched for one person, "I need you to say one true thing before Saturday. One. You keep saying you're fine, you keep making jokes, and honestly it's starting to feel like a performance for my benefit, like you think if you admit it's hard then I'll fall apart. That's not friendship, that's you deciding my feelings for me. That's basically solipsism with extra steps."

"That is not what solipsism means."

"It absolutely is. Look it up on the bus." Zaynab's chin was doing the thing it did before she cried or before she fought someone, and there was no way to tell which. "I've been rehearsing this all week. You're not the only one losing something here, Sierra. You get a new town. I just get an empty chair."

Sierra opened her mouth to say something light and competent and found nothing in stock. The lanterns buzzed. Somewhere inside, Malak turned the volume up, which was his way of giving them privacy. "I'm not fine," she said finally, and the words came out smaller than she'd planned, almost bellicose in their reluctance, like they'd been dragged to the yard against their will. "I keep telling people I am because it seemed like the adult thing, like the thing a person who chose this would say. My dad got the job, we're going, that's good, and I thought if I acted excited enough I'd become excited. It hasn't worked. I just get tired at nine p.m. and now I know it's twenty points, twenty and twenty, and I've been carrying that around like it's nothing."

Zaynab was quiet for a moment. Then she said, "See, and I spent all week being angry at you for leaving like it was optional, like you were choosing a new life over us, and I had this whole speech ready about how you'd forget us by October. But it's not even optional. Your dad's job. I've been furious at you for something you don't control." She wiped her face with the heel of her hand and laughed, wet and surprised. "I was going to make tonight a fight. I practiced the fight in the mirror."

"You practiced a fight and I practiced being fine," Sierra said. "We're quite a pair."

Malak leaned out the back door and yelled that they were doing the group photo before the last guests left, and Zaynab grabbed Sierra's wrist and pulled her toward the lanterns, and Sierra let herself be pulled, punch slopping over the rim of her cup onto the grass.

activity: to implement a binary search and explain why it beats a linear search on sorted data
knowledge_domain: to implement a binary search and explain why it beats a linear search on sorted data
fact: Programmers describe linear search as O(n), meaning its work grows in step with the list, and binary search as O(log n), meaning its work grows with the logarithm of the list's size.
story:
The whiteboard in the library's small study room had been wiped badly, so that a ghost of last week's chemistry equations floated behind the marker Jake was holding. He had written "O(log n)" near the top and then stopped, the way you stop when you've committed to a cliff.

"You have to actually say words," Noemie said. She had her laptop open on the long table, a sorted list of eight thousand library call numbers glowing on the screen. "The counselor thing. That's the whole point."

It had started as a joke. The library ran a coding hour on Saturdays for middle schoolers, and Ms. Bekele had asked Jake, Noemie, and Alexander to run it because the three of them were always in the building anyway, hogging the outlets. Then Ms. Bekele had gotten a grant for fifteen laptops, and suddenly the joke had a budget, and a sign-up sheet, and a room booked every week through spring. Next Saturday was the first session. The plan was to teach the kids to search a sorted list, and the three of them had to decide, by vote, whether to demo linear search or binary search. The rule, which Ms. Bekele had invented and enforced with a jaundiced eye from behind the circulation desk, was that nobody voted on anything they couldn't explain.

"Fine," Jake said. He uncapped the marker again. "Linear search is you start at the first shelf and check every single book until you find the one you want. Eight thousand books, worst case, eight thousand checks. Programmers call that O(n). The n is the list. The work grows in step with the list."

"Which is the exact word," Alexander said, without looking up from his own laptop, where he was losing at something with a leaderboard. "She made you write it down. I watched you write it down."

"I wrote it down, I didn't memorize the pronunciation of it." Jake drew a line under the shelf, split it in half, and circled the middle. "Binary search, you look at the middle first. The book you want is either before it or after it, so you throw away half the list. Then half of what's left. Eight thousand, four thousand, two thousand." He kept halving until the marker squeaked to a stop at one. "That's O(log n). The work grows with the logarithm of the list's size. Which is why it beats the linear one on sorted data, and why somebody wrote it on the board like a trophy."

"It was me," Noemie said. "I wrote it, you claimed it. Your culpability here is total."

Jake set the marker down. He had been thinking about it all week, on the bus, in the shower, in the middle of a history essay about something he could no longer remember. There was a part of him that liked linear search, liked its dumb honesty, the way it just put its head down and walked the whole aisle. Binary search felt like a trick, a cheat code, and he distrusted things that worked too well. But he had tested both, in the library's own catalog data, which Noemie had exported with Ms. Bekele's card and a promise. The linear version ground through the full list. The binary one blinked and was done, and it did it not because it was cleverer about books but because it refused to look at most of them.

"It only works if the data's sorted," he said slowly. "If you have to sort it first, you pay that cost up front. Like, if the kids search the same list a hundred times, you can amortize the sorting across all hundred searches and it's basically free. If they search it once, it's not." He looked up. "I don't know which one to vote for."

"That's the most honest thing you've said all afternoon," Alexander said.

"It's a vote on what to demo," Noemie said. "Not a vote on your soul."

Ms. Bekele appeared in the doorway with a cart of returns, having apparently decided the room had been quiet for too long. She looked at the whiteboard, at the halved line, at the phrase "O(log n)" sitting there like something that had wandered in from a different school entirely. "You can explain it to twelve-year-olds," she said. It was not quite a question.

"Half the middle schoolers are smarter than Alexander," Noemie said.

"Statistically defensible," Alexander said.

Ms. Bekele looked at Jake, waiting. He picked the marker back up, wiped the chemistry ghosts away with his sleeve, and wrote LINEAR and BINARY on opposite sides of the board, then the numbers underneath: 8,000 checks versus about thirteen, give or take, which he computed in the margin and double-checked, because being wrong in front of Ms. Bekele was not survivable.

"We demo both," he said. "We race them. The kids run the race, once with sorted data, once with shuffled, and they get to see the binary one lose the second time. Then they vote too." He capped the marker. "I'm abstaining on ours. I still can't decide if I trust a method that doesn't look at everything."

"That's called efficiency," Alexander said.

"It's called not looking at everything," Jake said.

Ms. Bekele pushed the cart past the door and paused. "Room's booked for the vote in ten minutes. Be rehearsed by then." She pointed at the whiteboard. "And put the marker back where it lives. It costs more than your lunches."

Noemie turned her laptop so the list faced the room. Alexander finally closed his game. Jake stood in front of the board with his hands in his pockets and began, quietly, to say it out loud: "So imagine eight thousand books, and you're only allowed thirteen guesses."

activity: to explain consent, contraception and how to get tested for infections at a clinic
knowledge_domain: to explain consent, contraception and how to get tested for infections at a clinic
fact: Condoms are the only common contraceptive method that also reduces the risk of sexually transmitted infections.
story:
Hayden had agreed to this before he understood what it was. The health center at his college ran a peer program, and the coordinator had emailed in June asking if he would train over the summer and lead workshops in the fall. He had said yes because the email made it sound like a T-shirt was involved. Now, in his grandmother's kitchen, a binder the size of a paving stone sat in front of him, and the first page said, in florid script that some administrator clearly thought was friendly: Welcome, Educator!

He had come to the grandparent's house because his own house was loud and this one smelled like toast and lavender, and because his grandfather could be trusted to nap through anything. He spent the first hour trying to collate the training sheets, which had been printed out of order, so that the page on clinic confidentiality ended up stapled to a crossword about trust. When he finally got them straight, he texted Magalie, because she was the only person he knew who would pretend to be a first-year student on demand.

She arrived with Hunter, who had not been invited but had never in his life allowed that to stop him. "We're your practice audience," Hunter said, taking a chair and a cookie without negotiating either. "I'm a confused freshman. Watch me be confused."

"Fine," Hayden said. "You're at a party. Someone hands you a drink, and then they're standing very close, and you want them to be standing very close, and you don't know what to say."

Magalie, in character, leaned toward Hunter. "Do you want to come outside with me?"

Hunter blinked. "Was that it? That was the whole move?"

"That's the whole move," Hayden said. "You ask. If the answer's yes, great. If the answer's anything besides yes, you take a step back and you don't act wounded about it. Consent isn't a plebiscite you win once and then govern forever, either. You can ask again later and get a different answer, and you have to be okay with that." He heard himself say it and thought, absurdly, that he sounded like a laminated poster. But Hunter was nodding, so maybe laminated posters knew something.

The trouble started at contraception. Hayden laid out the cards the training binder gave him, the pill, the ring, the IUD, the implant, condoms, and Hunter, still in character as the confused freshman, picked up the pill card and read it aloud with mock solemnity. "So this stops pregnancy."

"Right."

"And infections?"

Hayden opened his mouth to say yes, and then his mouth stayed open, because he genuinely did not know. He looked at the back of the card. It talked about hormones and schedules and nothing else. He felt the specific heat of being seventeen and confidently wrong in front of two people who would remember it forever.

"Okay," Magalie said. "This is the part where the peer educator says let's find out together, right? Isn't that in your binder?"

"It's in my binder," Hayden admitted. He found a page, and there it was, and he read it twice, and something clicked into place with an almost audible sound. "The pill doesn't protect against infections. Neither does the implant or the ring. Condoms are the only common contraceptive method that also reduces the risk of sexually transmitted infections. That's why the clinic hands them out even to people who are on something else." He set the pill card down and picked up the condom card and held them side by side like a magician revealing which card was the queen. "They do different jobs. One job is pregnancy. The other job is infections. Only condoms clock in for both."

"Say that at the workshop exactly like that," Hunter said. "Clock in for both. You'll get a standing ovation."

"The standing ovation part is the testing talk, actually, and I still have to practice it." He checked his notes. "So, testing. Clinics do it, it's usually quick, they can't tell your parents in most cases, and you can call ahead or just walk in. You don't need to be sick to go. Some infections don't announce themselves." He looked up. "That's what I've got. What I don't have is whether I'd actually say any of this to a room of strangers without my voice doing the thing."

"Your voice does a thing?" Magalie said, delighted.

"A thing," Hayden confirmed.

His grandmother came in then, surveyed the cards on her table, and put a plate of sandwiches down without a single question, which was its own kind of dignity. Hunter took one and raised it like a toast. "To the only condom on the payroll."

Magalie raised hers. "To the confused freshman."

Hayden raised his sandwich too, and then, because his grandmother was watching with an expression he could not read at all, he slid the cards into a neat stack and set them under the binder. She winked at him and turned the kettle on.

activity: voting in an election for the first time at eighteen
knowledge_domain: voting in an election for the first time at eighteen
fact: In Canadian federal elections, an eligible voter who is not on the voters list can register at their assigned polling place on election day.
story:
Addison woke on election morning with the small ceremonial weight of someone who had been waiting, without admitting it, for a date on a calendar. She was eighteen as of the ninth of the month, which meant that today, for the first time, she was allowed to do the one thing her civics teacher had called the minimum obligation of citizenship, a phrase Addison had resented even as she copied it down. She went to the kitchen table, where her mother was already sorting mail into two unsteady towers, and began looking for the voter card she assumed had arrived weeks ago.

It had not. She searched the recycling, the drawer of batteries and dead pens, the folder her mother kept for anything official. Ayanna had posted a photo of her own card on Monday, the fold crisp, the polling station printed in a tidy serif, and Addison had felt a private flare of pride seeing it, as if the card were a diploma. Now she sat at the table with her laptop open and nothing in her hands, and the feeling in her chest was closer to the dread of a lost permission slip than to anything civic.

"So register," her mother said, not looking up. "People do it at the door, don't they? They did in my day." Her mother's day, in this matter, was not a reliable source; she still believed the microwave interfered with the wifi. Addison wanted certainty, a rule she could point to, and it occurred to her that this was the first thing she had ever wanted as an adult that she could not ask a teacher to settle.

She typed the question herself and read, twice, the plain line on the Elections Canada page: an eligible voter who was not on the voters list could register at their assigned polling place on election day. She said it out loud, partly to believe it. "You can just show up," she told her mother. "At the right poll, on the day." Her mother shrugged as though Addison had announced that water was wet, but Addison copied the address of her assigned polling station onto the back of an envelope, along with a list of accepted ID, because trust in a website felt different from trust in a person, and she wanted both.

Alexia arrived at eleven, still in her coat, holding two coffees and an argument. She was working the campaign office phones until six and had come, she said, to collect Addison for a shift. "It's one day," Alexia said. "You can amortize your whole civic conscience across four years, but today is the day it costs something." Addison laughed despite herself. "You can't use amortize on a conscience." "I just did. You have to prove who you are anyway, at the poll." She raised her coffee in a small toast. "Go prove it."

They argued, in the friendly way that had survived four years of group projects, about whether a vote was a lever or a message. Addison had changed her leaning twice in six weeks, once after a leaders' debate and once after her mother, over dishes, described the childcare benefit that had let her go back to work when Addison was three. She could not make those two reasons sit together cleanly, and she was tired of pretending they did. "I might still be deciding in the booth," she admitted. Alexia said that was honest, which was the nicest thing she could think of to call indecision, and Addison chose to take it as a compliment. "You're so perspicacious," Alexia added dryly, "it's a wonder you can order lunch." That, at least, was clearly not a compliment.

What Addison had not planned on was the neighbor. Ms. Weber, from two doors down, knocked at two o'clock holding her own voter card and a casserole dish she claimed was "for morale," though whose morale was unclear. She wanted company walking to the poll; her knees were untrustworthy on the ice and her daughter was in Calgary. "You're on the list, are you?" she asked, and when Addison said no, not on any list, Ms. Weber's face did the thing older faces do when they are about to be reassuring. "You can register there," she said. "At the poll. Today. I've watched them do it." Addison nodded and said she knew, and felt, strangely, more certain having heard it from a person in a quilted coat than from the government's serif typeface. She went upstairs, of her own volition, to change out of the shirt she had slept in.

The line at the school gymnasium moved in pulses. Addison stood between Ms. Weber and a man reading a folded newspaper with the patience of someone who had voted in worse weather. When her turn came, she laid out her passport and a utility bill, answered a question about her address, and watched a woman behind the table write her name onto a sheet, unhurried, as though this were the most ordinary transaction in the world. Then the ballot, the cardboard privacy screen, the pencil on its string. She stood there longer than she meant to, the two reasons still not reconciled, and then made her mark.

Outside, the cold pressed against her face and Ms. Weber took her arm at the elbow, both of them careful on the ice. "Well," Ms. Weber said. "What did you do, girl? Don't tell me. Never tell anyone." Addison laughed, her breath going up white, and put the envelope, blank now, into her pocket.

activity: to argue both sides of a Supreme Court case about free speech before a mock court
knowledge_domain: to argue both sides of a Supreme Court case about free speech before a mock court
fact: The First Amendment limits what the government can do to speech; it does not by itself stop a private employer or private company from restricting speech.
story:
Joshua had taped his two outlines to opposite walls of his bedroom, which meant that arguing both sides of Tinker v. Des Moines for Monday's mock court involved a lot of walking. He paced from the government's wall to the students' wall, delivering the same paragraph twice with opposite convictions, and his father kept appearing in the doorway with a dish towel over his shoulder like a man checking on a strange animal.

"You're arguing against yourself," his father said.

"That's the assignment. Both sides, ten minutes each. Ms. González wants us to find out if we can hold two ideas at once." Joshua tapped the paper on the government's wall. "Schools can regulate speech if it materially disrupts learning. That's the whole case."

His father looked at the towel in his hands as if it might explain his son, then went back to the kitchen.

On Saturday Caiden came over with his laptop and a bag of chips he did not intend to share. He set up at Joshua's desk to edit a video the two of them had made for Miya's channel, a channel with eleven subscribers, nine of whom were people from their seminar class. Miya arrived an hour later, sullen about something, and stood in the doorway with her arms crossed until Joshua made room for her on the bed.

"They took it down," she said. "The platform. They said it violated community guidelines, which it did not, and when I appealed they just sent the same email twice. That is a violation of my free speech rights and I am going to sue."

Caiden didn't look up from the timeline. "You can't. It's a private company."

"It's my speech and they suppressed it."

"Sue them with what money," Caiden said. "You're in a state of personal insolvency. You borrowed lunch money from me on Tuesday."

Miya threw a pillow at him. Joshua caught it, mostly because he was pacing and happened to be in its path, and he stood there holding the pillow while something shifted in his head. He looked at the government's wall, then at the window, then at Miya.

"The First Amendment limits what the government can do to speech," he said slowly. "It doesn't by itself stop a private company from restricting speech. That's why the case I'm doing is about a school district and not about a website. The school is the government, basically. Your platform isn't."

Miya stared at him. "That can't be right."

He got his casebook off the shelf and found the page, and she read it twice, her jaw set tighter with each pass. Caiden leaned back in the chair with the satisfaction of a man watching a prediction come true, which did nothing to assuage Miya's mood. She put the book down and said that it was a stupid system, that the whole point of free speech was that nobody could take it away, and Joshua heard himself starting to agree with her and then heard the other wall calling.

"It's not that simple," he said. "Think about what would happen if private companies couldn't moderate anything. Every comment section, every feed. The government staying out of it is what lets them make their own rules, even bad ones."

"So my video is gone and there's nothing I can do."

"There's nothing the First Amendment does about it. Whether there's something else you can do, I don't know. Terms of service, maybe. I genuinely don't know."

She considered this the way she considered losing arguments, which was silently and at length. Then she picked up the casebook again and flipped past the page he'd marked, frowning at the language, and he realized she was reading ahead on his case, on both sides of it, which was more than Caiden had ever done.

That night, after they'd left, Joshua took the two outlines down off the walls and laid them side by side on the floor. He knelt between them. The government's argument was cleaner, better sourced, easier to admire. The students' argument was the one he actually believed, and he could not find a way to say so out loud without weakening it, because belief kept sliding in where evidence should stand. He read both paragraphs one more time, then turned off the lamp and lay down on the carpet between them, staring at the ceiling where the two walls met.

He was still there in the dark when his father came up to say goodnight, paused in the doorway, and decided not to ask.

activity: argument structures, nuanced reasoning and conditional thinking in abstract and hypothetical discussion
knowledge_domain: argument structures, nuanced reasoning and conditional thinking in abstract and hypothetical discussion
fact: A counterfactual conditional describes what would have been true if things had been different, such as 'if Sally owned a donkey, she would ride it', and usually implies the 'if' part is false.
story:
The bus pulled away from the stop at 7:42, and Vincent stood on the curb with his debate binder pressed against his chest, watching its rear doors fold shut. If he had left five minutes earlier, he would have caught it. He said it out loud on the walk to school, once to the empty street and once to Jessica when she fell into step beside him near the corner, her coffee steaming in the cold.

"If I'd left five minutes earlier," he said, "I'd be sitting on that bus right now instead of freezing."

"You can't check that, though," Jessica said. She handed him half her muffin without being asked, because she had seen him run out of his house with nothing but the binder. "You left when you left. There's no other version to go look at."

Vincent bit into the muffin and thought about that the rest of the way. It was a strange kind of sentence, the kind he was supposed to be good at by now, three weeks into his senior year and two days before the first debate of the season. It claimed to describe the world, but the piece of the world it described did not exist.

The debate room smelled like radiator dust and the oranges Ms. Chukwu kept in a bowl on her desk. She was writing the motion on the board in her looping hand: This house regrets the rise of unpaid internships. Zara was already there, voluble as always, arguing with the empty chairs about labor markets while she sharpened a pencil that did not need sharpening.

"You're negating with me," Zara said when Vincent sat down. "Which means you have to defend internships, or at least the world that has them."

"That's the part I keep getting stuck on," Vincent said. "We're not defending the actual world. We're defending a hypothetical one, where internships work the way the motion imagines."

Ms. Chukwu peeled an orange and let the peel fall in one unbroken spiral, which she could do and which neither of them had ever managed. "Debate runs on hypotheticals," she said. "The question is which kind you're using. Some claims you can test. Some you're just building in the air." She slid a segment of orange across the desk to each of them, and Vincent took his even though he wasn't hungry, because it was the kind of thing she did and the kind of thing you accepted.

After school, Jessica found him in the library with his notes spread across two tables, morphology charts from linguistics homework shoved to one end and debate cards to the other. "You look like a person who lost something," she said, dropping into the chair across from him.

"I found something, actually. This morning, with the bus. That sentence, if I'd left earlier, I'd have caught it. It's describing what would have been true if things had been different." He tapped his pen against a card. "And the thing is, it only works because we both know I didn't leave earlier. The false part is baked in. Zara says there's a name for it."

"There is," Jessica said. "Counterfactual conditional. We did it last week in logic." She pulled his card toward her and read it. "It's a whole genre of sentence. If Sally owned a donkey, she would ride it. And you just automatically hear that Sally doesn't own one."

"So in the debate," Vincent said slowly, "if I argue that internships give students access they wouldn't otherwise have, I'm building a counterfactual. Without internships, students would be shut out. But nobody can check that, because there is no world without internships to go visit."

Jessica leaned back. "Which doesn't make it useless. People reason like that all the time. You just have to be honest that it's a guess wearing a suit."

He worked until the librarian flicked the lights twice, and Zara found him at the door with her backpack already on. "I changed our second argument," Vincent told her on the steps outside, breath fogging. "We're not saying interns are better off than students with no internships, because we can't know that. We're saying the burden of proof goes the other way. The affirmative has to show that the alternative world, the one without internships, is actually better, and all they've got is the same kind of uncheckable sentence we have."

Zara squinted at him. "So we're conceding we can't prove our world is good?"

"We're arguing that certainty isn't on the table for either side, and the motion says regrets, which needs a comparison nobody can run." He pulled his gloves out of his pocket. "Ms. Chukwu's whole thing, right. Which claims you can test."

The morning of the debate, Vincent left his house twenty minutes early. The bus came at 7:37, and he sat near the front with his cards on his knees, and when the affirmative speaker stood up and said that without internships, students would enter the job market prepared and fairly paid, Vincent uncapped his pen and wrote across his flow pad, in letters large enough that Jessica, watching from the audience, could read them upside down: counterfactual. He underlined it twice, stood, and adjusted the microphone down to his height.

activity: graduating from high school
knowledge_domain: graduating from high school
fact: Pomp and Circumstance became graduation music after it was played at Yale's commencement in 1905, where Edward Elgar received an honorary doctorate of music.
story:
The trumpet felt heavier than usual, though it weighed the same two pounds it always had. Maelie stood in the school hallway outside the gym with the rest of the band, waiting to run Pomp and Circumstance for the fourth time that afternoon, and for the fourth time she wondered why every school in the country played the same song for graduation. Nobody had ever told her. Nobody had ever wondered, as far as she could tell. The senior class sat on the bleachers inside in their caps and gowns, rehearsing the process of walking slowly in a straight line, which turned out to be harder than anyone expected.

"Why this song?" she asked Mario, who played clarinet and knew, or claimed to know, the origin of most things.

"Edward Elgar wrote it," Mario said, which answered nothing.

"That's who wrote it. I asked why we play it. Every school plays it. There's no law."

Mario shrugged. "Tradition."

The word landed badly with Maelie, the way it always did. In chemistry that spring, Ms. Whitaker had taught them that a polymer was just a monomer repeated until it stopped being one thing and became another, and Maelie had thought at the time that tradition worked the same way, except that nobody could point to the first unit anymore. She had skipped a grade, which was why she was sixteen and graduating with people a year older, and which meant she had spent the year being either precocious or pitied depending on who was talking. She was tired of both. She wanted to know things for reasons she could defend.

Cassandre appeared from the gym doors in her gown, holding her phone. "They want us faster," she said. "Apparently we are funeral-paced."

"We are pacing the graduates," Maelie said. "If they walk fast, the whole thing takes eleven minutes and nobody's grandmother cries."

Cassandre expostulated that the whole thing took forty minutes regardless, that crying grandmothers were not the band's responsibility, and that she personally intended to walk at whatever speed she pleased, since she was graduating and Maelie was only in the band. This was technically true and also beside the point, so Maelie let it go.

After the run-through, while the senior class practiced standing up and sitting down in unison, Maelie sat against the lockers with her phone. She found the answer in an article about Elgar, and she read it twice because it seemed too small to explain so much. "It became graduation music," she told Mario, "after it was played at Yale's commencement in 1905. Elgar was there. He got an honorary doctorate of music."

"So one school in Connecticut ruined it for everyone," Mario said.

"Or made it," Maelie said, though she wasn't sure which, and that was the part that bothered her.

There had been a moment in ninth grade, before any of this, when she had stood in this same hallway holding a schedule with a mistake in it, too many classes, a sophomore course wedged into her freshman year. Her mother had said take it, it's a gift. A counselor had used the word "accelerate," as if she were a river carrying sediment downhill, alluvial, moving because gravity insisted. Maelie had liked the image then. Now she suspected the counselor had just meant faster, and that most impressive words meant faster if you checked. But she had taken the class, and the one after it, and here she was, sixteen, in a polyester gown's future, still playing other people's march while they walked.

Here was what she could not resolve: the song was beautiful, and it was worn, and those were not opposite conditions. The seniors in the gym looked solemn and ridiculous at once, and she could not separate the solemnity from the ridiculousness, and maybe she was not supposed to. She believed in asking why, and she had asked why, and the answer was that Yale played it in 1905 and Elgar got a doctorate, and the answer explained almost nothing about the girl crying in the third row of bleachers right now, whose name Maelie didn't know, who was leaving this town in August for a place she'd visited once.

Ms. Whitaker came down the hallway with the processional orders in her hand. "Places," she said. "One more time, from the doors."

Maelie stood, lifted the trumpet, and watched the doors swing open.

"Ready," she said. "Two, three, four."

activity: to plan a week of meals, shop for the ingredients and cook them in batches
knowledge_domain: to plan a week of meals, shop for the ingredients and cook them in batches
fact: Freezer burn happens when air dries out the surface of frozen food; it makes food tough and tasteless but does not make it unsafe to eat.
story:
Nicole had six days to fill her grandmother's freezer, and she was starting with a shopping list written on the back of a hospital parking receipt. The plan belonged to her mother, who had delivered it over the phone with the briskness of someone delegating a military operation: Grandma came home Saturday, she would be tired, she should not have to think about food. Nicole would plan the week's meals, shop for them, and cook them in batches so that everything needed only reheating. She had agreed partly out of guilt and partly out of a suspicion, which she kept to herself, that she was the only person in the family who would find it fun.

The fun lasted until she opened the chest freezer in the laundry room on Wednesday and found her trial batch of beef stew from Sunday. She had made it before she really understood what she was doing, portioned it into a container, and pressed the lid down with the confidence of a person who had never owned a freezer in her life. The surface of the stew now wore dry white patches, like frost that had decided to settle permanently, and Nicole stood over it with the container in both hands, calculating the moral mathematics of throwing out four dollars of beef.

She texted Lewis, who was unreliable in most matters but had worked a summer at a grocery store. "White dry stuff on frozen stew," she typed. "Throw it out?" His reply came in three installments, characteristically voluble even by text: first a photo of his own dinner, then "thats freezer burn," then, after she pressed him, "air dries out the surface when it gets in. it makes food tough and tasteless. but it doesnt make it unsafe to eat." She read this twice. Unsafe was the word she had been circling around all morning without naming it, and it turned out the problem was merely an aesthetic one, which felt simultaneously like a relief and like an insult. She had been prepared to impute to the stew some deep contamination, and instead it was guilty only of being badly sealed and dried out.

She put the container back and re-planned. Thursday she shopped properly, with Emmanuel, who insisted on coming along and turned out to be surprisingly useful in the produce section, holding up two onions and asking which one looked more like a Wednesday. He was, he admitted freely, there because he wanted to learn to cook before college and had no grandmother's kitchen of his own to practice in. He had a whole theory about it, something about wanting to arrive in the dorms as the person who could feed people. Nicole let him carry the carrots.

They cooked Friday. Emmanuel browned the chicken while Nicole portioned stew and chili into containers, pressing plastic wrap directly against the surface of each one before sealing the lids, because air was now her sworn enemy. She had drawn up a labeling system with dates and reheating instructions so elaborate that Emmanuel called it a controlled substance registry. "Your grandma is going to think she's been hospitalized in a restaurant," he said, and she told him that was the nicest thing anyone had said to her all week.

Mr. Quinn, the neighbor, appeared at the back door around four with a casserole dish covered in foil, which was a problem, because Nicole had not planned for other people's contributions and her labels did not have a category for them. "Freezer's getting full," he observed, peering past her at the stacked containers. He wanted, she realized, to be useful, the way neighbors at a time like this often did, and it seemed unkind to tell him that the freezer had reached its carrying capacity. She made space on the top shelf by consolidating two batches of soup, and Mr. Quinn left looking pleased with himself.

The stew with the white patches she had kept, in the end, partly out of thrift and partly as an experiment. She set it out Saturday morning to thaw, and when Lewis arrived that afternoon to help carry things, ostensibly, though he mostly sat on the counter and narrated, she reheated it along with the newest batch so that she could compare. "One of these is a crime scene," she warned him. "I'm not telling you which."

Grandmother came home at five, thin and voluble in a way that surprised them all, talking the entire way from the car about the hospital food, which she described as a controlled experiment in flavorlessness, an oxymoron she seemed to enjoy deploying. She toured the freezer with her coat still on, reading labels aloud, and pronounced the operation a triumph. Then she refused dinner. She was tired, she said; she would have some toast and go to bed; Nicole should take something home for her own mother, who had been driving back and forth all week.

So it was Nicole, Lewis, and Emmanuel who sat at the kitchen table at seven with the two pots of stew between them, and Lewis, who had served himself from the wrong one without asking, went back for seconds. "This one's better," he said, pointing at the container with the white patches. "It's got that dried-out texture."

activity: to apply a feminist or Marxist critical lens to a passage from a classic novel
knowledge_domain: to apply a feminist or Marxist critical lens to a passage from a classic novel
fact: Charlotte Brontë first published Jane Eyre in 1847 under the name Currer Bell, which did not reveal that its author was a woman.
story:
Victor would be the first to say he had the assignment under control, which was not entirely true, since it was Sunday night and the passage was due Monday morning and he had written nothing but his name. He sat cross-legged in the reading nook his mother had built into the corner of his room, a cushioned shelf above a radiator, with Jane Eyre open to the chapter where Rochester disguises himself as a gypsy to read the young women's faces. Ms. Crowchild wanted them to try a lens, feminist or Marxist, and write a page. Victor had told Abbas at lunch that the whole thing was obvious, patriarchal rich guy playing with poorer women, done, and he had mostly believed himself.

The copy he was using was not his. He had taken it from his grandmother's house on Saturday, from a shelf of books with cracked spines, because his own copy was still in Byron's car. This one smelled of dust and pencil shavings, and when he turned past the title page he stopped. "Jane Eyre: An Autobiography. Edited by Currer Bell." He ran his thumb over the name. Below it, "London, 1847." He texted his grandmother's landline was useless, so he tried the group chat instead.

Abbas replied first. who is currer bell, and Victor typed back what he had worked out from the tiny print on the facing page, the editor's note his grandmother had pencilled an arrow beside years ago: "Charlotte Brontë first published Jane Eyre in 1847 under the name Currer Bell. It didn't reveal that the author was a woman." He stared at the message after he sent it. He had read that chapter three times for class and never once wondered who was allowed to put a name on the front.

Byron's message arrived as three thumbs-up and then, a minute later, "so she had to lie to get published?" Victor started to answer no, that wasn't lying exactly, and then deleted the draft, because he wasn't sure. He was often not sure in ways he didn't admit at lunch, where he preferred to be the one explaining things to Abbas, who was quieter, and to Byron, who was louder but lazy in a way that let Victor shine. He looked at the passage again. Rochester in his false cloak, telling fortunes, handling Blanche Ingram's hand like a purchase he was evaluating, while Jane sits half in shadow and he does not read her palm at all.

The feminist reading came easily now, almost too easily, and Victor distrusted things that came easily. A man who owns the house, the servants, the party, and the women's attention besides. But the pseudonym kept snagging him. Brontë could not publish as herself, and the book she published under a mask was about a masked man exercising power in his own drawing room. The two ideas fit together in a way he could not yet phrase, and he had a page, not an essay. He wrote on a sticky note: who is disguised here, and who chose the disguise?

His mother knocked and left tea on the shelf without a word, which was her way of noticing he was working without interrupting him, and he mouthed thanks at the closing door. He drank it too fast and burned his tongue.

He tried the Marxist lens on for size. Jane is a governess, paid to be in the room but not of it, her labour invisible so that the leisure of others can exist. That was true and he could prove it from the text. But it didn't account for the moment Jane speaks back to Rochester, plainly, refusing the fortune-teller's game, and Victor liked that moment too much to grind it down into a thesis. He remembered Abbas saying quietly, once, when the class was arguing about whether Jane was a role model, "She doesn't have to be anything for us." Victor had sardonically called that a cop-out at the time, out loud, and regretted it, and regretted it again now, sitting with the book that proved Abbas kind of right. The inheritance at the end, the uncle's money arriving to lift Jane into independence, sutures the whole romance shut; her freedom arrives as patrimony, unearned and dropped from above, and Victor could not decide whether Brontë knew that and let it sting, or whether the ending was just the shape the market allowed a woman's novel to take in 1847. He wrote that sentence down and thought it was probably the best thing he'd ever written and definitely stolen, in spirit, from somebody.

He texted Abbas: "you were right about Jane. sort of. explain at lunch." Then, because it was late and Monday was coming and the page was still mostly empty, he opened a fresh document and typed a first line: "The man in this chapter wears a disguise he chose; the author of the chapter, to publish it at all, wore one too." It wasn't a thesis. It was a door he hadn't walked through yet. He read it twice, put his grandmother's book gently face-down on the radiator, and picked up his pen.

activity: to use a geographic information system to overlay flood risk and housing on a city map
knowledge_domain: to use a geographic information system to overlay flood risk and housing on a city map
fact: Roger Tomlinson led development of the Canada Geographic Information System in the 1960s, the first computerized GIS, and is often called the father of GIS.
story:
Paige had the laptop open on the kitchen table and the tutorial paused at minute four, because minute four assumed she already knew what a layer was. Outside, the window showed the ordinary street, the ordinary gutter, the ordinary puddle that formed every spring in the same low spot by the mailbox, which was the whole reason she had chosen this project. Her geography teacher had offered a list of topics, and Paige had picked the one where she could prove something about her own neighborhood instead of somewhere she had never been.

The software was called QGIS, and it was free, which her mother appreciated, since the motherboardboard of the old laptop had already been replaced once. Paige had a shapefile of the city's floodplain, downloaded from a county website at eleven at night, and a second file of housing parcels, color coded by whether they were owner occupied or rentals. The tutorial said to drag one on top of the other. Hers went beside the other, then behind it, then somewhere off the coast of a neighboring state. She closed the map, reopened it, and started over.

Charly texted a picture of their own project, a poster about erosion with a drawing of a sad cliff. "At least I can draw a cliff," Charly wrote, when Paige complained. Paige sent back a screenshot of her map, which now showed the floodplain as a blue smear with the housing layer completely invisible beneath it. "Yours looks like a weather report for the whole earth," Charly said. Myah, added to the group, said only, "ask mr yoon," which was Myah's answer to most things, though in fairness Mr. Yoon did keep office hours on Thursdays and did seem to enjoy them.

Paige did not want to preempt her own discovery by asking an adult the answer first. She was aware this was slightly ridiculous, like refusing to look up a word in a dictionary on principle, but she had learned the hard way in ninth grade that a teacher's explanation arrived fully smooth, with all the interesting rough edges of figuring it out already sanded away. So she opened a browser tab instead and typed "GIS history," mostly to procrastinate, partly because the tutorial kept using the acronym like it was a person she should already know.

The first result was a photograph of a man in a suit, and the caption said Roger Tomlinson. Paige read it twice. In the 1960s, in Canada, he had led the development of the Canada Geographic Information System, and it was the first computerized GIS. The article called him the father of GIS. She sat with that for a second, the phrase sitting oddly in her head, father of a system, as though software had a family tree. She typed it into the group chat. "did you know the guy who made the first one was canadian," she wrote, then, more carefully, for Myah, who liked precision: "roger tomlinson, in the 1960s. the canada geographic information system. first computerized gis. they call him the father of gis." Charly replied with a single maple leaf emoji, which Paige chose to interpret as reverence.

It put things in a strange light, actually. She was sitting at a kitchen table with a free program on a dying laptop, dragging files around with a mouse, and sixty years ago someone had built the first version of this from scratch, on machines that probably took up a room. She went back to the tutorial with a kind of borrowed patience, and this time she understood what the narrator meant by transparency, that the blue flood layer could be thinned until the parcels showed through underneath, the way you could see the bottom of a pond if the water wasn't so determined to be a color.

Then the map assembled itself. The floodplain followed the creek two blocks north, which she knew, and it lapped down over three streets of apartment buildings, which she knew less well. Her own building sat just outside the blue, close enough that the margin looked thinner than her thumbnail. The rentals were almost entirely inside the flood boundary. The owner occupied houses were almost entirely outside it, up the gentle hill she had walked a hundred times without ever thinking of it as a hill.

Her mother came home at six with a bag of groceries and the news that the landlord had raised the rent again, forty dollars, which was forty dollars that would not be going in the envelope her mother sent to her grandmother every month without fail. Paige had heard the word remittance for the first time that year, in a class about migration, and had recognized it as the name for something her family had been doing all along. She turned the laptop so her mother could see the map. "See where the blue is," Paige said. "That's where it floods. Now look at which buildings are in it."

Her mother set down the groceries and looked for a long moment, the way she looked at bills. "Nobody tells you this in those letters from the county," she said finally, meaning the flood notices that came in envelopes Paige had always assumed were junk mail. Her mother tapped the screen near their own building, in the thin margin outside the blue. "And this part, how sure are they?"

Paige was honest, because that was the only position she had that was worth anything. "I don't know yet," she said. "The line is an estimate, and I haven't found what year the data is from, or how they drew it." She had a lot more map to make before she could put her own street on it with any confidence. Myah had texted again, a single question mark under Paige's fact about Tomlinson, and Charly had sent the maple leaf a second time, as though for emphasis. Paige saved her project, twice, in two places, and started digging through the county website for the metadata file.

activity: going on a first date
knowledge_domain: going on a first date
fact: Psychologists call it misattribution of arousal when a racing heart caused by fear or excitement is mistaken for attraction to the person nearby.
story:
Lily had told herself she would be calm about this, and for most of the afternoon the promise held. Then the doorbell rang at four, and it was Destiny, carrying boots and a bag of hairpins and the loose, conspiratorial energy of someone who considered herself an expert in matters she had never once experienced.

"You're not wearing that," Destiny said, which was facetious, because Lily was wearing the gray sweater she always wore, and Destiny had seen it a hundred times.

They ended up on Lily's bed with the laptop between them, watching a horror trailer Destiny insisted would "set the mood," though for what mood she didn't say. On screen a woman walked backward down a hallway, and somewhere behind the soundtrack a door hinge complained. Lily felt her heart kick, quick and shallow, and she laughed to cover it, and Destiny laughed too, and neither of them looked away from the screen.

The trailer ended and Destiny laced her boots without looking up. "You know my sister's doing psych," she said. "Psychologists call it misattribution of arousal. When your heart races from fear or excitement, you can mistake it for being attracted to whoever's standing nearby." She pulled the lace tight. "So if you feel dizzy on this date, check whether there's a ghost in the room first."

Lily said something dry about Destiny's romantic advice, but the sentence had landed somewhere under her ribs and stayed there. Because her heart had been doing that kick all week, since Tuesday, since Reid's text, and she had filed it under nerves, and now the file wouldn't close.

Reid arrived at seven, exactly on time, holding a paper bag of the licorice she'd mentioned once, months ago, in a hallway conversation she hadn't known he was storing. From downstairs her mother's voice carried up, bright and overacted, and Lily stood at the top of the stairs listening to Reid answer questions about his college plans in that careful, flattened way he had with adults, and she thought: I don't feel anything. Her chest was quiet. She descended slowly, testing it, the way you test a loose tooth.

They walked to the pond and back because neither of them drove yet and the movie theater was closed for renovations, and the date, if it was one, consisted of cold air and a bench and long silences that Lily kept trying to read. He talked about the bowling league, about a tiebreaker he'd lost the previous Saturday, how his hands had shaken on the last frame. She watched his mouth move and performed interest while a private argument went on inside her, one she conducted with Destiny's sister's textbook logic as her only witness. The trembling before dates, the flutter in the hallway on Tuesday, the sleepless Wednesday. Fear or attraction. Arousal or alarm. She had assumed they were the same thing wearing different coats, that the flutter was just terror of the evening ahead, and now she sat on a bench beside a boy she had chosen clothes for and felt, distinctly, nothing. Her heartbeat was a metronome. The doubt, which had been small, began to metastasize, spreading from the evening into the whole past month, so that even Tuesday's text seemed suddenly harmless, ordinary, a boy bored on a bus.

"I should tell you something," Reid said, and the pace of everything changed, the way a room changes when a match is struck. He turned the licorice bag over in his hands, once, twice. "I almost didn't come tonight. I've been telling myself for a month that you think of me as, like, a teammate. And then I thought, if that's true, no harm done, and if it's not." He stopped. A dog barked somewhere behind the reeds, and Lily's heart went off like a struck bell, sudden and total, and in the same instant she understood that the dog was behind her, the fear was elsewhere, and the bell was still ringing. The trailer, the bench, the boy. She had the timeline wrong all along. The flutter had started Tuesday, before any ghost in any hallway, before fear had any excuse to exist.

"Say something," Reid said. "Please. You're doing the face."

"I did the math wrong," Lily said. He frowned. She was already reaching for his sleeve. "I'll explain later. Or never. Come here."

activity: saying goodbye to a grandparent who has died
knowledge_domain: saying goodbye to a grandparent who has died
fact: Margaret Stroebe and Henk Schut's dual process model describes grieving people as moving back and forth between facing the loss and getting on with rebuilding daily life, rather than moving in one direction.
story:
The casseroles had been arriving since eight in the morning, and by noon the kitchen counter at his grandmother's house had become a geography Daniel could read like a map: the lasagna from the aunties, the samosas from Ms. Santoso next door, the store-bought cookies nobody would admit to bringing. He moved through the crowd of relatives with a plate he wasn't eating from, nodding at condolences the way you nod at customs officers. His grandfather had been dead for six days. Everyone kept asking whether he was holding up, and Daniel had discovered he didn't know, because holding up implied a direction, and he couldn't find one.

He slipped into the den, where his grandfather's chess set still sat mid-game on the folding table by the window. His grandfather had left it that way on purpose, the old man claimed, so that Daniel would have to come back and finish it. Daniel sat down and studied the board without touching anything. His phone buzzed. It was Saif, who had skipped the funeral because of his chemistry exam, asking whether there was food, whether there were girls, whether Daniel had cried yet. Daniel typed back a maybe, deleted it, and then, feeling like a misanthrope for hiding while his grandmother stood alone in a room full of people, he pocketed the phone and went to find her.

In the living room his cousin was showing Eshal, who had come with her mother, a video on her phone. It was some TikTok of a cat falling off a counter, and the sound that came out of Daniel was a real laugh, sudden and whole, before he even decided to make it. Eshal glanced at him and smiled. Then the laugh curdled in his chest. Six days. His grandfather's chair was still at the table with the newspaper folded on it, and here he was laughing at a cat. He muttered something about the bathroom and went back down the hall, his face hot, trying to metabolize the guilt alongside the lingering warmth of the laugh, the two refusing to dissolve into each other.

In the den he sat on the floor with his back against the bed and texted Saif the truth: he'd laughed at a video and now he felt like garbage. Is that normal, he wrote. He stared at the little gray bubble for a long time, listening through the wall to the murmur of relatives trading stories about his grandfather, the good ones, the ones where the old man cheated at cards and blamed his glasses.

In the kitchen, Ms. Santoso was helping Daniel's grandmother wrap leftovers in foil, her hands moving with the ease of twenty years of borrowed sugar and returned dishes between their houses. She had watched the boy move through the rooms all afternoon, the way he hovered at doorways, and she thought of her own father's funeral in Jakarta, how her brother had spent the whole reception in the garden and everyone had called it disrespect when it was anything but. She caught Daniel's eye through the doorway and gave him a look that said, plainly, come here, and he did, because she was the kind of adult who never made you perform.

His phone buzzed in his hand. Saif had sent a paragraph, then a second one, then the link to a psychology page he'd clearly found in ninety seconds of desperate searching. "It's called the dual process model," the first message read. "Margaret Stroebe and Henk Schut."
