She tapped each page as she counted. "Edinburgh, St Andrews, Durham, Manchester, Leeds, Bristol, and this one at KCL. Seven. If I cut two, I'm deciding something at eighteen that I can't take back, and the form doesn't even care which one I want most. It just wants five." Her voice had gone flat, the way it did when she was frightened of wanting something.

He pulled his chair over beside her. "What are the two at the bottom?"

"That's the trap. There is no bottom. They're unordered. Bristol and Manchester, maybe, but Manchester has the module on migration policy, and Bristol has the girl I met at the open day who said I could stay with her in first year, which is a terrible reason, I know it's a terrible reason."

The library hummed around them, low and industrious. Two tables away a man read a newspaper, and Isaac caught the word subpoena in a headline about a council inquiry before the man folded the page over. Below the window, a primary school group crossed the car park in crooked pairs. Isaac had known Noelle since year ten, when she had been the most voluble person in their form, narrating everything, and he had liked that, and lately she had gone quieter and he did not know whether the change was in her or in what they were doing to themselves this year.

"Okay," he said. "Forget the courses. Tell me what you'd study if nobody was grading you."

She looked at him like he'd handed her a riddle. "Migration. Displacement. Where people go and what they're allowed to be when they get there."

"Then that module isn't a bonus. It's the thing." He slid Manchester out of the fan and put it on top, then remembered and flattened it back level with the others. "Sorry. No order. But you know now."

"And Bristol?"

"Cut it. You can visit the girl. You don't need to enrol near someone to be friends with them." He paused. "And cut St Andrews. You only put it there because your mum did."

"She'll be devastated."

"She'll be devastated for a week. You'd be at the wrong university for three years." He said it and heard his own case underneath it, his five choices sitting somewhere in a server in England while a stranger decided, and the whole thing had been fermenting in him since December, this not-knowing, and Noelle's problem was easier than his because at least hers could be solved by noon. "Look, I'm not saying it's clean. I'm saying Manchester and migration is the honest one, and the rest is decoration."

She gathered the Bristol and St Andrews pages, held them a moment, then tore them once, not dramatically, just along the fold, and put the halves in her bag. The remaining five she stacked and clipped. "It's done, then. Five. No order, all equal, and I want one of them more than anything." She laughed, briefly. "That's allowed, right? Wanting one more?"

"Nobody checks," Isaac said.

Mr. Ramos came by on his rounds with the trolley of returns and paused at their table. "You two look like you've finished something. Nobody in this building looks like that in January." He took in the clipped pages, the closed laptop, Isaac's hand resting on the trackpad.

"Course choices," Noelle said. "He untangled it."

"Then I'll leave you to the next tangle." He pushed the trolley on toward the stairs.

Noelle stood, shouldered her bag, and hesitated. "When yours comes through, whatever it is, text me first. Before anyone."

"First," Isaac said. She went down the stairs and he heard the door at the entrance swing, then shut. He opened the laptop. The portal still said under consideration. He looked at it for a while, then logged in to the UCAS page he kept bookmarked and read, for the third time this week, the line about five courses, no order of preference, as if it might have changed while he wasn't watching.

activity: going on a first date
knowledge_domain: going on a first date
fact: In a 1999 study, Tanya Chartrand and John Bargh found that people liked a partner more when that partner quietly mimicked their posture and gestures, even without noticing the mimicry.
story:
The bleachers were already loud when Samuel arrived, which he preferred, because loud meant Coraline wouldn't hear how carefully he was breathing. He had read about the study two nights ago, at one in the morning, in a psychology textbook his brother had left behind: in 1999, Tanya Chartrand and John Bargh found that people liked a partner more when that partner quietly mimicked their posture and gestures, even without noticing the mimicry. It had seemed like a cheat code. Now, watching the kickoff from the far side of the field, he wasn't sure whether it was clever or dishonest, and he had promised himself he would only do it if it felt natural, which was a standard so vague it could justify anything.

He found her near the concession stand, wearing her brother's old varsity jacket, and after the first awkward minutes of the game she settled her elbows on the rail in front of them, chin in her hands. Samuel waited a count of three, then set his elbows on the rail too, chin in his hands, and stared at the field as though deeply invested in a sport he did not understand.

Maksim appeared in the second quarter with nachos and no date, which was normal. He stood beside Samuel and talked about a tangential theory involving the referees and money, then lowered his voice. "You're copying her."

"Copying who."

"Her arms. Same arms." Maksim crunched a chip and watched the two of them with the frank interest of someone observing an experiment. "That's weird, dude. Or is it a thing? Is that a thing people do?"

"It's a study," Samuel said, quietly, because Coraline had gone to get hot chocolate and could come back at any moment. "1999. Tanya Chartrand and John Bargh. People liked a partner more when the partner mimicked their posture and gestures, and they never even noticed the mimicry."

"So you're doing science."

"I'm being agreeable."

"Same thing in this town," Maksim said, and went to find better seats.

What Samuel did not know was that Coraline had stopped at the top of the ramp, holding two hot chocolates, and had heard most of it. She had thought about simply returning with the drinks and pretending otherwise. Instead she stood for a moment above the bleachers, in the cold, and considered the shape of the evening differently than she had all week.

She had liked Samuel since September, in a way she hadn't wanted to examine too closely, because examining things had a way of making them smaller. But this changed the question. If he was engineering her liking him, then what exactly was she responding to, the boy or the trick? And yet, she reasoned, turning the paper cups in her hands, he had also confessed it, in public, to Maksim, which was either clumsy or brave, and probably both. When she was honest with herself, which she tried to be at least on weekends, she could not decide whether she wanted him to stop doing it or to keep doing it so well she never found out.

She walked back down and handed him his cup. Then, instead of resting her elbows on the rail, she sat on the bench, sideways, one leg tucked under her, and watched to see how long it would take him to follow.

Samuel felt the shift like a trapdoor. He cogitated furiously for what was probably four seconds, the crowd roaring over some touchdown he missed entirely, and understood that he had been caught, or else that he hadn't and this was coincidence, and that there was no way to know which, and that this not-knowing was going to be the ordinary condition of every honest relationship he ever had. He sat down. Sideways, one leg tucked under him, even though his other leg had fallen half asleep and it hurt.

"Comfortable?" Coraline said.

"Very," Samuel said, and his face went red, and he laughed at himself before she could.

She looked at him for a long moment over the rim of her cup, and then she leaned forward, elbows on her knees, and waited. The scoreboard flashed, the home crowd screamed, and after a moment Samuel leaned forward too, elbows on his knees, cup balanced in both hands, holding her eyes the whole time.

activity: moving to a new town and leaving old friends behind
knowledge_domain: moving to a new town and leaving old friends behind
fact: In May 2023, US Surgeon General Vivek Murthy issued an advisory describing loneliness and isolation as an epidemic in the United States.
story:
The house smelled like paint and nothing else, which was somehow worse than the smell of old cigarettes or boiled dinner, because at least those smells meant somebody had lived there. Carson sat on the floor of his empty bedroom with his phone and a sandwich his mother had made from a cooler, since the fridge wouldn't be delivered until Thursday. The movers had left at four. It was six-thirty now, and outside the window there was a street with three other new houses on it and a fourth half-built, its skeleton of two-by-fours silhouetted against a sky that had no opinion about him at all.

He had three bars of signal, which felt like a personal achievement. He texted Jaiden a photo of the empty room with the caption "my new palace," and Jaiden replied within a minute with a photo of the senior parking lot and the words "found a spot, you'd have hated it." That was the whole exchange. It was funny and it was also like pressing on a bruise to check that it still hurt, which Carson did twice more before putting the phone face-down on the floor.

The trouble was that he couldn't decide what he was actually supposed to do next. His father's position, delivered over the cooler sandwich, was that this was an opportunity, and that Carson would make new friends within two weeks because he always did, a claim based on evidence from when Carson was nine. His mother's position was quieter, which was that he was allowed to be sad about it, but that being sad in a house this empty was going to echo, so maybe find something to do. Neither position was wrong. Neither was useful either.

He wandered downstairs. In the living room the previous owners, or possibly the builders, had left a radio on the counter by the microwave that wasn't installed yet, sitting there on a plywood slab with its cord coiled like it was waiting to be needed. He found a battery in the junk drawer, which already existed, which meant junk drawers preceded actual furniture, which he found quietly hilarious. The radio crackled and found a station mid-sentence.

"Murthy," the voice was saying, "the Surgeon General, issued an advisory back in May of this year, 2023, describing loneliness and isolation as an epidemic in the United States."

Carson sat down on the plywood counter with his legs dangling, because there was nowhere else to sit. The host went on to something else, some politician's response, but the sentence stayed with him the way a fact does when it lands at the exact wrong-right moment. An epidemic. He had always thought of epidemics as things that showed up on graphs with steep red lines. Loneliness as a thing you could catch, or that could catch you. He didn't buy it entirely, either. Calling it an epidemic felt like it might pathologize something ordinary, the way his health teacher in tenth grade had tried to make everything a symptom. Plenty of people were alone and fine. Erin, for instance, spent most of lunch alone with a book and seemed more solvent than anyone else he knew, though when he'd said that to Jaiden once, Jaiden had pointed out that Carson had never actually asked Erin about it, which was true and annoying.

But he was sitting in an empty house in a town where he knew the radio better than any person, and the advisory had named the thing accurately enough that he felt seen by a government document, which was a new experience. He thought about what Ms. Ma had said at the end of last year, in the last class of senior seminar, when a kid asked what philosophy they should take to college. She'd said, "Don't take a philosophy. Take two, and make them argue." She'd written the word existentialism on the board and then, next to it, the names of three people who thought the whole enterprise was sentimental nonsense, and assigned them all. At the time it had seemed like a dodge. Now it seemed like the only honest instruction he'd ever been given.

So he tried it. Position one: he needed people, tonight, and calling Jaiden would fix that, and there was no shame in it, since apparently the Surgeon General agreed the condition was widespread enough to warrant paper. Position two: a person who called old friends the first night in a new town was just refusing to start, and starting was the whole assignment, and clinging to Jaiden like a security blanket would make the next town, and the one after that, each harder than the last. Both positions had merit. Neither conceded.

He picked up the phone anyway, and while it rang he noticed he'd already decided something, which was that it didn't have to be either-or. He could call Jaiden and still knock on the door of the house across the street tomorrow, where he'd seen a kid about his age carrying boxes in, badly, dropping a lampshade and looking around to check whether anyone had seen. There was a version of this that wasn't a security blanket. Maybe it was even, in some small unheroic way, altruistic, since Jaiden had found a parking spot he'd have hated, which meant Jaiden was keeping score on an empty chair.

"Tell me about the parking spot," Carson said when Jaiden picked up.

"It's between a truck with a Trump sticker and a truck with a Bernie sticker," Jaiden said. "They've formed an alliance. It's beautiful."

Carson laughed, and in the empty living room the laugh came back to him off the bare walls, and outside, in the half-built house across the street, a light came on where there hadn't been one before.

activity: to implement a binary search and explain why it beats a linear search on sorted data
knowledge_domain: to implement a binary search and explain why it beats a linear search on sorted data
fact: The first known mention of binary search in computing was by John Mauchly in 1946, in the Moore School Lectures, an early course on electronic computers.
story:
Vanessa had promised the coding club she could teach binary search in eight minutes on Thursday, and by Tuesday she still did not know how to make it feel like anything more than a diagram. So she spread her materials across her grandmother's kitchen table, between the sugar bowl and a plate of lemon squares: her laptop, a marker, a stack of one hundred index cards she had numbered from one to one hundred and shuffled into a shoebox. The plan was to have someone find card seventy-three. She could make them flip through one at a time, calling out each number, and then she could show them the other way, the way that halved the world every time it asked a question. The problem was that she could explain the steps and still not explain why anyone should care, and Mr. De Vries, who ran the club, had told her that a demo without an argument was just a magic trick.

Her grandmother drifted past with a watering can and paused at the chaos of cards. "You are finding something," she said.

"I'm practising. I have to explain it to people who think it's boring."

"Which people?"

"Anas thinks anything with a proof is boring. Maxime thinks anything she already knows is boring. Between them, I have maybe four minutes of goodwill."

Her grandmother set the can down and picked up a card, turned it over, put it back. "When I was a girl we had one telephone directory for four towns. You did not read it. You opened it in the middle and looked at your thumbs."

Vanessa stopped with her hand in the shoebox. She had been pred icating the whole lesson on the assumption that her audience needed computers to care about searching, and here was her grandmother describing exactly the method without ever having called it anything. "Wait. Say that again?"

"Open in the middle. If your name comes before, you throw away the back half. Then the middle again. Three times and you are at the page." Her grandmother shrugged, as if confessing to a small theft. "Everyone did it. Nobody taught it. It was just faster than being stupid with a phone book."

For the rest of the afternoon Vanessa made her grandmother be the demo. She wrote the numbers one to one hundred on cards, sorted them, and had her hunt for a target with linear search first, while Vanessa counted the flips aloud. Fifty-nine flips. Then she had her halve the pile, and it took seven. Seven against fifty-nine, and her grandmother laughed at the difference like it was a joke someone should have told her forty years earlier. Vanessa wrote the numbers in her notebook and underlined them twice, because numbers a person had watched happen were different from numbers in a textbook. Somewhere in there, watching her grandmother's thumbs hover over the deck, Vanessa asked herself a question she could not yet answer: was the idea old because computers were old, or was it old because impatience was old?

That evening she opened her laptop at the kitchen table to draft the talk, and her grandmother watched over her shoulder while pretending to dry a spoon.

The poster for Thursday was already made, and that was the other problem. The club was building a timeline of algorithms to hang outside the computer lab, and on Monday it had caused a genuine argument. Maxime had marched a strip of paper across the whole length and written SORTING at the far left, on the grounds that people had sorted things since Babylon. Anas had moved the strips around with the truculent certainty of someone losing a board game, insisting that searching had to be older, because you had to find a thing before you could sort it, and the two of them had gone back and forth until Mr. De Vries said they needed evidence, not vibes. Vanessa had been assigned the searching side. What she had so far was a stack of web pages that mostly disagreed with each other, and one forum post with no sources, which claimed binary search dated to the 1940s. She wanted the first real mention, not a rumor.

She found it in a scanned set of lecture notes, late, while her grandmother peeled an orange two feet away. The first known mention of binary search in computing was by John Mauchly, in 1946, in the Moore School Lectures, an early course on electronic computers. She read the page twice, then a third time, partly to be sure and partly because something about it pleased her. She said the name out loud. "The Moore School Lectures."

"That's where it starts?" her grandmother asked.

"That's the earliest one anybody can point to. Nineteen forty-six. John Mauchly." Vanessa copied the citation into her notebook, then sat back and looked at the index cards, which were still stacked in their sorted little city on the table. The idea in the cards and the idea in the lecture were the same idea, and yet one of them lived in her grandmother's thumbs and the other in a room full of engineers in 1946, and she could not decide whether that made the idea older or younger than either date. She decided she would say exactly that to the club, that the timeline was true and also not the whole truth, and that she was comfortable leaving the rest unsettled. Mr. De Vries would hate it. Anas would love it. Maxime would demand a source, and for once Vanessa could hand her one.

On Thursday the room smelled like the rain everyone had tracked in. Mr. De Vries pinned the timeline to the corkboard while chairs scraped into a rough circle, and Anas arrived late, shaking water off his jacket and off his argument, which he had clearly rehearsed in the shower. Maxime had brought printed evidence for sorting, pages of it, and laid the pages down like a winning hand.

Vanessa put the shoebox in the middle of the table. "Before the timeline," she said, "I need a volunteer to find card seventy-three."

Anas reached for it, and Maxime reached faster. Vanessa handed her the shuffled deck first. "Linear search. Flip one at a time. Count out loud."

Maxime flipped, counting, and the count ran past thirty while the room got interested in her suffering. When she found the card at flip fifty-eight, Vanessa took the deck, sorted it in front of them, and gave it back. "Now halve it. Look at the middle card, decide which half is dead, throw that half away."

Maxime's hands did what grandmother-thumbs had done for decades, and the count stopped at six, and Anas said, quietly, "Do it again."

"That's Thursday's whole trick," Vanessa said, and pulled the strip of paper and the marker toward her. "Now. Searching. The first known mention in computing is John Mauchly, 1946, in the Moore School Lectures." She wrote it and stepped back. "But my grandmother found names in the phone book the same way her whole life, and nobody gave her a citation."

Maxime looked at the strip, then at the shoebox, then at Vanessa, and slid her whole stack of Babylonian evidence an inch to the left to make room.

activity: to argue both sides of a Supreme Court case about free speech before a mock court
knowledge_domain: to argue both sides of a Supreme Court case about free speech before a mock court
fact: In West Virginia v. Barnette (1943), the Supreme Court ruled 6-3 that public schools cannot force students to salute the flag or recite the Pledge of Allegiance.
story:
Michael had claimed the sunporch of his grandmother's house as his war room, spreading the case file across the wicker table where she used to take her morning coffee, and by late afternoon the pages had begun to curl in the heat. The mock court competition was in nine days. He was assigned to argue both sides of a free speech case, a fictional one his coach had built around a student suspended for refusing to stand during a school ceremony, and the problem that gnawed at him was not that he couldn't find arguments. It was that he kept believing whichever side he had most recently read.

"You look like a lawyer who lost his own case," his grandfather said, setting down a glass of lemonade and settling into the chair opposite. He had watched the whole thing from the kitchen window, apparently, and now he wanted a report.

"I have to argue that the school can make her stand," Michael said, "and then, an hour later, argue that it can't. Same girl, same ceremony. How do I do that without lying one of the times?"

His grandfather sipped his tea and said nothing for a while, which Michael had learned was not disapproval but something more like patience with a hinge that hadn't swung yet. "When I was your age," he finally said, "I changed my mind about a person once a week. It's not lying. It's trying the door from both sides to see which one the house wants you to use."

That evening Celeste came over with her laptop and her notebook full of arrows, and she took the other wicker chair without being invited, which was the arrangement between them. Serena arrived twenty minutes later with printouts she'd gotten from Mr. Adebayo, the history teacher who had agreed to advise their team even though, as she put it, he mostly just raised one eyebrow and handed you documents, which was his way of making you work.

Serena tapped the printout. "You keep building the school's side from scratch. There's a case. West Virginia versus Barnette, 1943. The Supreme Court ruled six to three that public schools cannot force students to salute the flag or recite the Pledge of Allegiance."

Michael read the highlighted paragraph twice. He noticed his own resistance first, a small flare of disappointment, because he had spent the afternoon constructing an argument that the case now seemed to gut. Then the more curious feeling arrived, the one he liked better: the question of how the Court had gotten there, and whether six votes out of nine meant the principle was solid or only barely solid, the way a bridge that holds is still worth checking.

"So the school side is dead?" Celeste said.

"No," Michael said slowly. "It's harder. That's different." He was already seeing the shape of it. On one side, Barnette; on the other, whatever the school could claim about order, ceremony, the rights of an institution as against a person. He started making two columns on the legal pad, and for the first time the two columns looked like two honest things rather than one true thing and one performance.

The next two days he proselytized to anyone who would listen, including the cashier at the pharmacy and his grandmother while she shelled peas on the porch. He would argue the student's side with all the fervor he had, then stop mid-sentence and say, "But wait, now hear the school," and do it again. His grandmother listened with her hands moving through the bowl and said only, "You argue prettier for the girl." That stung a little, because it was true, and he went back to the porch that night trying to locate the difference. What he found, in the lamp light with the moths ticking against the screen, was that his best argument for the school was not really about the school at all. It was about the other students, about a room full of people watching one person refuse something they had all done, and whether a community had any claim on its members' bodies. He wrote it down. He didn't know yet if it won. He only knew it was the version a person could hold without smirking.

On Friday Mr. Adebayo came by after practice, which he had never done before, and sat on the porch steps eating one of the grandmother's biscuits while Michael ran both sides for him straight through. When it was over, the teacher was quiet long enough that Michael started counting, got to eleven, and stopped.

"Your Barnette side is tight," Mr. Adebayo said. "Trenchant, even. The school side, you're apologizing for it in your tone. Judges hear apology before they hear argument." He brushed crumbs off his knee. "You don't have to love a position to believe it deserves its day."

Michael turned that over all weekend. He liked the word solvency, which he'd found in an old debate manual in his grandfather's study, the idea that an argument should actually fix the thing it claims to fix, and he began testing both his sides against it. The student's side, he thought, solved the girl's problem. The school's side solved something larger and vaguer, a thing about cohesion that he couldn't quite get to hold still, and he was honest with himself that maybe it wasn't solvable, maybe cohesion was a word people used when they meant comfort. He marked that passage in his notes with a question mark instead of a strikeout, because he wasn't ready to decide.

The night before the competition, Celeste and Serena came for a final run-through, and they made the sunporch into a courtroom, Serena presiding with a wooden spoon, Celeste flipping between the two stacks of pages as Michael switched sides mid-drill. "Same facts," Celeste said, shuffling. "Different world."

"That's what's strange," Michael said. "I keep expecting the facts to pick a side for me. They just sit there."

At the end of the last run, well after dark, his grandmother came out with a plate of sandwiches and stood a moment in the doorway, listening to the last exchange. Michael finished his rebuttal, closed his folder, and looked up at all of them, the spoon, the pages, the sandwiches.

"All right," Serena said, raising the spoon. "Which side wins?"

Michael said, "Ask me tomorrow," and reached for a sandwich.

activity: moving to a new town and leaving old friends behind
knowledge_domain: moving to a new town and leaving old friends behind
fact: A 2018 study by communication researcher Jeffrey Hall estimated it takes roughly 50 hours of time together to turn an acquaintance into a casual friend.
story:
Victoria sat on the floor of the empty living room with her phone balanced on her knee, because the movers had taken the last box an hour ago and there was nothing else to sit on. The new house smelled like paint and cold air. In three days she would start at a school where she knew nobody, in a town she had chosen for her mother's sake and not her own, and she had spent the whole drive telling herself it would be fine, which had stopped working somewhere around the second highway exit.

A knock came at the open front door and a man in a cardigan leaned in, holding a kettle. "I'm Mr. Hussain, from next door. The last family left this behind and I thought, new people, first night, no kettle." He set it on the counter, which had no counter yet in any meaningful sense, just plywood and dust. He nodded at the phone. "Reading the obituaries, or worse?"

"Articles about friendship," Victoria said, before she could decide whether to admit it. "There's a study from 2018, some communication researcher, Jeffrey Hall. He estimated it takes roughly fifty hours of time together to turn an acquaintance into a casual friend."

Mr. Hussain considered this the way people consider weather. "Fifty hours. That's more than it takes to learn to drive." He looked around the empty room. "Well. The kettle boils in about three minutes if you ever need company." Then he was gone, and Victoria felt obscurely better, the way she did when something private turned out to be a thing other people could say out loud.

The first week of school she collected acquaintances the way her father collected parking stubs. Two girls adopted her at lunch by the second day, Tea, who drew aliens in the margins of her chemistry notes, and Joy, who knew where the vending machine gave two drinks for one. They were kind, and Victoria did the math anyway. Fifty hours. A school week gave you maybe six hours of actual together time, lunch and the walk to the bus and the dead air before class. At that rate she would have a casual friend by November, and she had left behind Mariam, with whom she had eleven years of accumulated hours, and she could not decide whether the arithmetic was comforting, because it meant nothing was wrong with her, or terrible, because it meant the clock simply did not care.

Her mother, querulous by the end of each moving-box day, asked why Victoria hadn't invited anyone over, and Victoria said the house had no chairs, which was true and also a dodge. What she did not say was that she had started to wonder whether she was commodifying the whole thing, pricing friendship in hours like a currency, when the hours she remembered best with Mariam had been wasted ones, afternoons with no purpose at all, the kind that felt like they didn't count until they turned out to be all that counted. Maybe the study measured something real and she was reading it like a contract. Maybe both. She held the two ideas side by side and could not get them to merge.

In the third week, Tea found her after last period sitting on the wall outside the gym, and sat down without asking, which was the first thing anyone had done that hadn't felt arranged. "Joy's mom has the car and won't be done at the dentist till five," Tea said. "You want to just sit here and be bored with me?"

"I'm actually good at that," Victoria said. Tea drew an alien on the back of Victoria's hand with a pen, and gave it a speech bubble that said it was new here too. They sat for over an hour, and Victoria noticed she had stopped counting minutes somewhere in the middle, and noticed that not noticing felt different from having it all fixed, and let that be enough for one afternoon. Later she would tell her mother about the study, fifty hours, casually, the way Mr. Hussain had heard it, and her mother would say that sounded about right, and Victoria would still not know whether right meant true.

At home the kettle worked. She made tea in a chipped cup and carried it next door, and when Mr. Hussain opened the door she said, "Three minutes, you said. I'm cashing in."

He stepped back to let her in, already reaching for his own cup.

activity: how a bill becomes a law through drafting, committee review, debate, votes and assent
knowledge_domain: how a bill becomes a law through drafting, committee review, debate, votes and assent
fact: Under the US Constitution, if the president neither signs nor vetoes a bill within ten days, Sundays excepted, while Congress is in session, it becomes law without a signature.
story:
Jordyn had the corner computer by the window, the one with the wobbly chair, because it was the only station where the screen didn't face the aisle and nobody could see her refreshing the same page. The page was Congress.gov, and the bill was H.R. 2140, which her government teacher had assigned as "track a bill through the semester," and which Jordyn had picked for reasons she hadn't written in the assignment sheet. The bill would let people found innocent after a federal conviction claim restitution for the years they had lost. Her brother Marcus had spent fourteen months in a county jail before the whole case collapsed, and although the bill wasn't about people like him, not exactly, it was the closest thing on the list to a sorry.

The library smelled like the photocopier warming up and someone's wet umbrella. Mr. Gagnon, the reference librarian, drifted past with a cart of returns and paused. "That looks like homework," he said, in the tone of a man who had decided homework in his library was a good thing.

"Tracking a bill," Jordyn said. "It's in drafting still. They keep changing the language." She pointed at the amendments stacked under the text, each one a little cleaner or a little blunter than the last. "Two weeks ago it said 'compensation.' Now it says 'restitution.' I like that word better. Compensation sounds like a paycheck."

Mr. Gagnon nodded slowly, as if she'd said something worth taking home. "Let me know if the site locks you out. It does that after forty minutes," he said, and rolled the cart toward biography.

By October the bill had a number of co-sponsors and a hearing before the House Judiciary Committee, and Jordyn had a routine. Tuesdays and Thursdays after school, the wobbly chair, one granola bar split with whoever showed up. Nickolas showed up most often, because he was tracking a bill about highway funding and needed somewhere to sit that wasn't his house. Gary came when his debate team needed evidence, and he would read over Jordyn's shoulder with his chin practically on her collarbone until she shoved the granola bar at him.

At the committee hearing, which she watched on the library's ancient tablet with the cracked screen, Jordyn learned that the hard part wasn't writing the bill, it was surviving it. A witness from a prosecutors' association said the bill would invite people to litigate hopeless claims for a payday. A woman who had served nine years for a crime she didn't commit said, quietly, that nine years had no payday. The committee marked the bill up, cut a section, restored it, and voted it out on a Thursday night while Jordyn was technically supposed to be home for dinner.

The floor debate was where it got ugly. Gary read the transcript aloud in a low voice, doing the voices, and Jordyn laughed even though the words were about whether innocent people deserved anything at all. Then the vote, 231 to 197. Then the Senate's own version, its own committee, its own amendments, and a month of nothing while Jordyn refreshed the page until the page number seemed to burn into the screen.

In April both chambers had passed the same words, and the bill went to the president. Jordyn assumed there would be a signature, a pen, one of those photos. Instead the days passed and nothing happened. Day four, day six, day nine. She refreshed until Mr. Gagnon said, gently, "It'll still be there tomorrow." On day eleven, the status line changed: the bill had become law. She sat back so fast the wobbly chair nearly dumped her.

"He never signed it," she said. "Look. It says it became law anyway." She scrolled, and there it was, in the flat language of the site: if the president neither signs nor vetoes a bill within ten days, Sundays excepted, and Congress is still in session, the bill becomes law without his signature. Nickolas leaned in and counted on his fingers. "So the Sundays don't count toward the ten." "Right," Jordyn said. "And if Congress had gone home, it would have just died quietly instead." She'd been so focused on signatures that she had missed the whole other road, the one where silence could mean either death or law depending on the calendar. It seemed like cheating, and then it seemed like the opposite of cheating, like the system admitting that a bill passed by both houses shouldn't vanish just because one man wouldn't pick up a pen.

She printed the status page for her assignment, and then, because it wasn't for the assignment, she printed the section on restitution and folded it into her backpack for Marcus. She imagined handing it over. She imagined him reading it, maybe smiling, maybe saying something about finally. When she got home he was on the couch with his headphones in, and she held the folded page out between them.

Marcus pulled out one earbud. "What's this?"

"The bill I was tracking. It's a law now. It's about restitution, for people like..." She stopped, because he was already shaking his head, slow and certain.

"I don't want to litigate anything," he said. "I just want to not talk about it." He put the earbud back in, and the folded page sat there between them on the couch, both of them looking at it, neither of them reaching for it.

activity: to plan a week of meals, shop for the ingredients and cook them in batches
knowledge_domain: to plan a week of meals, shop for the ingredients and cook them in batches
fact: A UN Environment Programme report found that 1.05 billion tonnes of food were wasted in 2022, and about 60 percent of that waste happened in households.
story:
The zucchini had gone soft in the drawer, and Cohen held it up like evidence at a crime scene. Behind it, a bag of spinach that had liquefied, half a cabbage gone grey at the edges. Fourteen dollars of produce, he estimated, transformed into something he was afraid to lift with bare hands. He took a photo before throwing it all out, mostly so he would have to look at it later.

At school, he'd been given the assignment on Tuesday: plan a week of meals, buy the ingredients, cook them in batches. Ms. Le had said it was about systems thinking, whatever that meant, and had refused to say more. "Figure out what breaks," she'd told the class, "and fix that." Cohen had assumed the hard part would be the cooking. It was not. The hard part, he was discovering, was that he shopped like a person imagining a life rather than a person living one. He bought the vegetables of an imaginary version of himself, one who came home energetic at six and julienned things.

He found Parsa at the farmers' market on Saturday morning, standing at a table of bread with a canvas bag over one shoulder. Parsa worked a checkout three summers running and treated markets like a second home. "You're back," Parsa said, sardonic. "Did the cabbage defeat you, or did you defeat the cabbage?"

"You heard about that?"

"Viviane has a group chat. There were photos." Parsa picked up a loaf, put it down, picked it up again. "What are you actually making this week?"

Cohen unfolded his list, which he had rewritten twice on the bus. Four dinners, cooked Sunday in two sessions, eaten in rotation. He explained the logic of it: buy only what the plan used, cook it before it could turn, and nothing sat in the drawer long enough to develop opinions.

"Planning as a cure for guilt," Parsa said. "Bold." But he walked the stalls with Cohen anyway, and when Cohen reached for two bunches of carrots without counting them, Parsa asked how many the recipe needed, and Cohen put one back, and something about that small correction felt like learning an instrument.

They found Viviane near the tomato table, arguing gently with a vendor about seconds, the bruised fruit sold cheap in paper bags. She bought three bags. "For sauce," she said, when she saw Cohen looking. "You roast them tonight, they're gone by Tuesday. Otherwise they're garbage by Wednesday."

"That's the thing," Cohen said. "I looked it up after my drawer situation. A UN Environment Programme report found that 1.05 billion tonnes of food got wasted in 2022." He paused, checking the number in his head. "And about 60 percent of that happened in households. Households. Not restaurants, not farms. Kitchens like mine."

Viviane considered this while bagging her tomatoes. "So it's not a supply problem. It's a Sunday problem."

"What?"

"Everyone's fridge on Sunday is a promise," she said. "By Friday it's a threat."

Cohen laughed, then stopped laughing, because it was too accurate. He had been thinking of the waste as a moral failure, his personal softness with zucchini, but it was also structural, a design flaw in how he moved through a week. You could proselytize about food waste all day, and he had, at dinner on Thursday, until his father asked him to pass the salt. But preaching didn't soften a cabbage. A plan did. At the same time, he wasn't sure the plan would survive contact with a real week, with rehearsal running late, with the evening he wouldn't feel like eating dal again. Systems held until they didn't. He said this out loud, and Viviane shrugged.

"Then the system includes nachos," she said. "Every good system has a pressure valve."

Here was the twist he hadn't expected: when they carried everything to the community booth at the market's edge, the one that collected unsold food for the shelter, the volunteer behind the table was Ms. Le, in an apron, weighing crates of squash. She raised an eyebrow at his full bags but said nothing about the assignment, and asked only whether he knew how to store fresh herbs, and he admitted he did not, and she demonstrated, a damp paper towel, loose wrapping, and turned back to her scale without a lesson attached.

That evening Cohen roasted Viviane's tomatoes, portioned dal into five containers, and labeled them with a marker that was almost out of ink. The fridge, when he stood back and looked at it, resembled a small argument for order. He took a photo of that too.

"Save that one for the chat," Parsa texted, when he sent it. "Redemption arc."

activity: to write a research paper with an argument, footnotes and a bibliography in a standard citation style
knowledge_domain: to write a research paper with an argument, footnotes and a bibliography in a standard citation style
fact: Chicago style offers two citation systems: notes and bibliography, common in history and the humanities, and author-date, common in the sciences.
story:
Ms. Ito handed the papers back on Thursday, face down, which everyone knew was a bad sign. Jasmine turned hers over and found the grade at the top, then a red circle around her first citation, then a note in the margin that said only: "Wrong system. See me."

She sat at the kitchen table that night with the paper flattened in front of her, her laptop open beside it, and a mug of tea going cold at her elbow. Her little brother had been sent upstairs. Her mother was working the late shift. The kitchen was quiet enough that she could hear the refrigerator humming, and she hated the refrigerator for it.

The paper itself had been fine. That was the galling part. Ninety pages of reading about the WPA Writers' Project, three weeks of Saturday mornings in the library, an argument she actually believed in: that the slave narratives collected in the 1930s were shaped by their interviewers more than historians had admitted. She had found two historians who disagreed with each other and had tried to hold both of them in her head at once, which was harder than writing anything down. Ms. Ito had written "good tension here" beside that paragraph, and Jasmine had looked at those three words for a long time before looking at the red circle again.

The circle was around a footnote. She had footnotes. She had a bibliography. She had done everything the handout said, or she thought she had, and she'd used the format from a chemistry lab report she'd found online, author and date in parentheses, because it looked clean and she could collate all her sources into one tidy list at the end. It had taken her two hours on a Sunday. It had felt like finishing.

She opened the school handbook and searched for "Chicago." The page that loaded talked about two systems. She read the sentence three times, certain she was misreading it. Two. One was called notes and bibliography, and the search result said it was the one common in history and the humanities. The other was called author-date, common in the sciences. She had picked the science one for a history paper. She had done it because the parentheses looked tidy, and tidiness had felt like rigor, and apparently those were not the same thing at all.

She texted Myla, who was in the other section and had gotten her paper back too.

"What did you use," Jasmine typed. "For citations."

"Footnotes at the bottom," Myla answered, fast, as though she'd been waiting to be asked. "Then a bibliography at the end. Nico did the author-date thing with the parentheses. Ms. Ito circled his too."

Jasmine put the phone down. So it wasn't only her, and somehow that made it worse, because it meant the mistake was reasonable, and reasonable mistakes were the ones that caught smart people.

She sat with the handbook open and her marked-up paper beside it and tried to watch herself the way Ms. Ito was always telling them to, some word from October floating back to her, metacognition, thinking about your own thinking, which Jasmine had privately considered a profligate waste of class time until this exact moment at the kitchen table. She had not thought about her sources at all. She had thought about formatting them, which was clerical, and she had let a choice that was actually about her whole paper happen by accident, by aesthetic preference, at eleven at night.

And there was something else, too, that she circled in pencil on the handbook page. The humanities used footnotes because historians argued in their citations, buried qualifications and disagreements down at the bottom of the page where there was room for them. The parentheses said only who and when. She had written a paper about two historians disagreeing and had cited them in a style that gave them no room to do it. She wasn't sure that was true, exactly. It felt true in a way she couldn't fully check, and she wrote a question mark beside it instead of pretending she'd proven anything.

She got out a fresh stack of note cards. She started with the first source, an article from 1988, and typed the number one at the bottom of the page and built the note the way the handbook showed, slowly, checking each comma.

Her phone lit up. Myla again: "Are you redoing all of them."

"Every single note," Jasmine typed back, and reached for the next card.
